I have been working this land for thirty years. My body knows the rhythm of this place — wheat goes in when the air turns cold, maize follows after the June harvest. I do not change what works. With some family members earning wages in town, I cannot count on having help whenever I need it, so I plan my inputs and timing carefully to reduce trips to the field and avoid crises.

**On wheat:** I will plant all 5 mu in late September or early October. I buy improved certified seed from the township supply station — locally adapted varieties yield better than whatever old seed I might save, and the price difference is small. I know from experience that wheat here needs three waterings: once before winter sets in, once at jointing, once at heading. With the well, I can manage this myself. I will apply base fertilizer before planting — compound fertilizer with phosphorus and potassium mixed in — then topdress urea at jointing. I have seen neighbors overdo nitrogen and get lodging; I keep my rate steady. Two pesticide passes: herbicide early and one fungicide spray at heading when powdery mildew risk is high.

**On maize:** Right after the wheat combine leaves the field in June, I direct-seed maize with no-tillage. It saves me two days of work and keeps moisture in the ground. I only use hybrid seed — that is simply how maize is done now, and the yield difference is real. Maize is hungry for nitrogen, so I put some down with the seed as base fertilizer and topdress heavily at the big bell stage. Corn borer is my main pest worry; I will spray once for that and once for weeds early on. If July rains are poor, I run the well once at tasseling. If rains cooperate, one irrigation at planting may be enough.

My priorities are stable yield, reduced labor, and keeping costs manageable since off-farm income is our main cushion this year.
